title: Air in Action
subject: Science
description: What air is made of, how air supports burning (the fire triangle, flame colour, miners' lamps, candles under jars), how air exerts pressure (straws, breathing, ears, altitude) and how wind, sea breezes and the monsoon are made.

questions.topic: Air is a Mixture of Gases
questions.question: According to the book, air is best described as
questions.explanation: The book says air feels like one thing but is actually made up of several gases mixed together, each present in a different amount.

questions.topic: Air is a Mixture of Gases
questions.question: In the '100 cups of air' picture, how many cups would be filled with nitrogen?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is the largest part of air: 78 of every 100 cups.

questions.topic: Air is a Mixture of Gases
questions.question: In the '100 cups of air' picture, how many cups would be filled with oxygen?
questions.explanation: Oxygen fills about 21 of the 100 cups; it is the gas our body needs.

questions.topic: Air is a Mixture of Gases
questions.question: Which gas in air has an amount that changes all the time, with more near the sea and very little in a desert?
questions.explanation: The amount of water vapour varies: more cups near the sea or in the rainy season, very few in a desert.

questions.topic: Air is a Mixture of Gases
questions.question: Which gas in air do plants use with sunlight to make their own food?
questions.explanation: Less than one cup of air is carbon dioxide, but plants use it with sunlight in photosynthesis.

questions.topic: Air is a Mixture of Gases
questions.question: Which gas is present only as a small trace and 'doesn't react with anything, it simply exists quietly'?
questions.explanation: Argon is the small trace left over; it does not react with anything and is just part of the mixture.

questions.topic: Air is a Mixture of Gases
questions.question: Where would you expect to find the MOST cups of water vapour in air?
options: Near the sea in the rainy season
In the middle of a dry desert
questions.explanation: The book says water vapour increases near the sea or in the rainy season and is very low in a desert.

questions.topic: Air is a Mixture of Gases
questions.question: Which list puts the gases in order from MOST to LEAST in air?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is 78 cups, oxygen 21 cups and carbon dioxide less than one cup.

questions.topic: Air is a Mixture of Gases
questions.question: The 100-cups activity asks you to imagine
options: sorting the air so each cup holds one gas
each cup holding the full mix of gases
boiling the air until it becomes water
counting the dust grains in every cup
questions.explanation: The idea is to sort all the gas so each cup contains just one gas; that shows how much of each gas is in air.

questions.topic: Air is a Mixture of Gases
questions.question: If nitrogen and oxygen fill 99 of the 100 cups, the last cup is shared by
options: only argon and nothing else at all
argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour
extra oxygen that was left over
only water vapour and nothing else
questions.explanation: The small remainder of air is made of argon, carbon dioxide and a changing amount of water vapour.

questions.topic: Air is a Mixture of Gases
questions.question: The book says air fills
options: even the empty corners of a room
only the spaces high in the sky
questions.explanation: Air is all around us; it fills spaces around trees, buildings and even the empty corners of a room.

questions.topic: Air is a Mixture of Gases
questions.question: Air is one single substance that is the same everywhere.
questions.explanation: False. Air is a mixture of several gases, and the amounts can even change from place to place.

questions.topic: Air is a Mixture of Gases
questions.question: Nitrogen fills about 78 of every 100 cups of air.
questions.explanation: True. Nitrogen is the biggest part of air at about 78%.

questions.topic: Air is a Mixture of Gases
questions.question: Oxygen makes up about half of the air around us.
questions.explanation: False. Oxygen is only about 21 cups out of 100, not half.

questions.topic: Air is a Mixture of Gases
questions.question: Carbon dioxide fills more cups of air than oxygen does.
questions.explanation: False. Carbon dioxide is less than one cup in 100; oxygen is 21 cups.

questions.topic: Air is a Mixture of Gases
questions.question: Which TWO gases together make up about 99 of the 100 cups of air?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen (78) and oxygen (21) add up to 99 cups; argon and carbon dioxide are tiny amounts.

questions.topic: Air is a Mixture of Gases
questions.question: Select the TWO true statements about carbon dioxide in air.
options: It is less than one cup in 100
Plants use it with sunlight to make food
It is the gas our muscles need to work
It is the largest part of the air
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide is a tiny part of air, used by plants in photosynthesis. Oxygen powers muscles and nitrogen is the largest part.

questions.question: About what percentage of the air we breathe IN is oxygen?
questions.explanation: Our lungs extract the ~21% oxygen from each breath and send the rest back out.

questions.question: About how much oxygen is in the air we breathe OUT?
questions.explanation: Exhaled air still has about 16% oxygen; we do not use up all the oxygen we inhale.

questions.question: About how much carbon dioxide is in the air we breathe out?
questions.explanation: Exhaled air has about 4% carbon dioxide, produced by your cells.

questions.question: What fraction of exhaled air is nitrogen?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen goes in and out unchanged, so exhaled air is still about 78% nitrogen.

questions.question: Why do we actually need nitrogen in the air?
options: To power our muscles, brain and heart
To help green plants make their food
To make candle flames burn brighter
To keep oxygen from being too concentrated
questions.explanation: Nitrogen dilutes oxygen. Pure oxygen continuously is toxic to cells, so the unreactive nitrogen provides safe dilution.

questions.question: What happens if a person breathes pure oxygen continuously over time?
options: It becomes toxic to the cells
The lungs stop needing to breathe
questions.explanation: The book states that pure oxygen continuously is toxic to cells over time, which is why we need diluted oxygen.

questions.question: Which statement about breathing is CORRECT?
options: Our lungs use up every bit of oxygen we breathe in
Air is mostly nitrogen; we use only part of its oxygen
Air is mostly oxygen because that is what we need
We breathe in pure oxygen and breathe out nitrogen
questions.explanation: A common mix-up is thinking we breathe pure oxygen. Air is 78% nitrogen, and exhaled air still has 16% oxygen.

questions.question: Compared with the air you breathed in, the air you breathe out has
questions.explanation: Exhaled air has less oxygen (16%), more carbon dioxide (4%) and more water vapour than inhaled air.

questions.question: Which gas does your body need to power your muscles, brain and heart?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is the gas your body needs to power your muscles, brain and heart.

questions.question: Exhaled air has about 4% carbon dioxide. Where does this carbon dioxide come from?
options: It is produced by your cells
It leaks in from the outside air
The lungs make it from water vapour
questions.explanation: The carbon dioxide in exhaled air is produced by your cells and carried out when you breathe.

questions.question: What would happen if nitrogen were NOT diluting the oxygen in the air?
options: Things would catch fire too easily
questions.explanation: Nitrogen keeps oxygen from being too concentrated; without it, things would catch fire too easily.

questions.question: The air you breathe out contains 0% oxygen.
questions.explanation: False. Exhaled air still contains about 16% oxygen.

questions.question: Our lungs take oxygen from each breath and send the rest of the air back out.
questions.explanation: True. The lungs extract about 21% oxygen and send the rest back out.

questions.question: Without nitrogen in the air, things would be LESS likely to catch fire.
questions.explanation: False. Nitrogen dilutes oxygen; without it things would catch fire too easily.

questions.question: Breathing pure oxygen all the time would be good for our cells.
questions.explanation: False. Pure oxygen continuously is toxic to cells over time.

questions.question: Select the TWO true facts about exhaled air.
questions.explanation: Exhaled air: ~78% nitrogen, ~16% oxygen, ~4% carbon dioxide and more water vapour than inhaled air.

questions.topic: Gases from Air and Their Uses
questions.question: Where, according to the book, is air separated into different gases?
questions.explanation: In factories, air is separated into gases like nitrogen, oxygen and argon and stored in cylinders.

questions.topic: Gases from Air and Their Uses
questions.question: Which gas is used in welding to protect the hot metal?
questions.explanation: Argon protects the hot metal from air during welding, keeping the joint strong.

questions.topic: Gases from Air and Their Uses
questions.question: Which gas is used to fill car and truck tyres?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen keeps the tyre pressure steady, even when the tyre gets hot on the road.

questions.topic: Gases from Air and Their Uses
questions.question: Which gas is used in hospitals to help patients breathe?
questions.explanation: Oxygen cylinders help patients who have trouble breathing on their own.

questions.topic: Gases from Air and Their Uses
questions.question: Why is argon used in welding?
options: It helps the metal pieces melt more quickly
It cools the metal down as soon as it is joined
It protects hot metal from air, keeping the joint strong
It makes the torch flame much hotter than usual
questions.explanation: Argon does not react, so it shields the hot metal from air and the joint stays strong.

questions.topic: Gases from Air and Their Uses
questions.question: Why is nitrogen used to fill truck tyres?
options: It makes the tyre much lighter than air would
It stops the rubber from ever wearing out
It helps the tyre grip the wet road better
It keeps tyre pressure steady when the tyre heats up
questions.explanation: Nitrogen keeps the tyre pressure steady even when it gets hot on the road.

questions.topic: Gases from Air and Their Uses
questions.question: Separating air into nitrogen, oxygen and argon in factories is given as proof that
options: air is a mixture of gases
air is a single pure gas
questions.explanation: If air can be split into separate gases, it must be a mixture, not one substance.

questions.topic: Gases from Air and Their Uses
questions.question: A cylinder is being connected to a welding torch to protect the joint. Which gas is most likely inside?
questions.explanation: Argon is the gas used in welding; nitrogen goes into tyres and oxygen into hospital cylinders.

questions.topic: Gases from Air and Their Uses
questions.question: In the pie-chart activity, if the whole pie is 100 parts, the oxygen slice should be about
questions.explanation: Oxygen is about 21 of 100 parts; nitrogen is 78 and all the rest share about 1 part.

questions.topic: Gases from Air and Their Uses
questions.question: What is welding?
options: Filling tyres with a steady gas
Joining two metal pieces with a torch
questions.explanation: The book explains welding as joining two metal pieces together with a torch.

questions.topic: Gases from Air and Their Uses
questions.question: Gases separated from air are stored in separate cylinders for later use.
questions.explanation: True. Nitrogen, oxygen and argon are stored in separate cylinders and used whenever needed.

questions.topic: Gases from Air and Their Uses
questions.question: Oxygen is used to fill truck tyres because it keeps the pressure steady.
questions.explanation: False. Nitrogen, not oxygen, is used to fill car and truck tyres.

questions.topic: Gases from Air and Their Uses
questions.question: Argon is used in hospitals to help patients breathe.
questions.explanation: False. Oxygen is used in hospitals; argon is used in welding.

questions.topic: Gases from Air and Their Uses
questions.question: Which TWO uses of gases from air are described in the book?
questions.explanation: The book describes argon in welding, nitrogen in tyres and oxygen in hospitals.

questions.question: What does the caver's small beeping device check?
options: The gases in the air around the caver
How many tools the caver carries
How much water the caver has left
How bright the headlamp is shining
questions.explanation: The device checks the gases in the air, making sure oxygen is enough and carbon dioxide hasn't built up.

questions.question: Where does the composition of air usually stay steady?
options: In open spaces where wind blows freely
Deep inside caves with still air
In closed rooms with poor ventilation
questions.explanation: Near open spaces where wind blows freely, air stays about 78 nitrogen, 21 oxygen and a little of the rest.

questions.question: In closed, still places where air cannot mix freely, oxygen can
questions.explanation: In closed spaces oxygen can drop and other gases can build up without anyone noticing right away.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed in the book as a place where the air balance can quietly change?
questions.explanation: Caves, crowded places, poorly ventilated rooms and sealed grain bins are listed; open windy places keep a steady mix.

questions.question: The caver's device makes sure that
options: oxygen is enough and carbon dioxide has not built up
nitrogen is low and argon is high enough
the cave is dry and the ropes are strong
there is enough light to see the walls
questions.explanation: It checks that oxygen is still enough to breathe and carbon dioxide hasn't built up too much.

questions.question: Why is the device so important even if a caver leaves everything else behind?
options: The device also works as a torch
Air changes can happen without anyone noticing
Caves are always completely dark inside
Ropes and helmets are easy to replace
questions.explanation: Oxygen can drop and other gases build up quietly in closed spaces, so a device is needed to notice the danger.

questions.question: Besides the beeping device, what do cavers carry into a deep cave?
questions.explanation: Cavers carry ropes, helmets, headlamps and the small beeping device.

questions.question: A classroom is packed with students and the windows have been shut for hours. Using the book, what can happen to its air?
options: Nitrogen slowly turns into fresh oxygen
The air becomes just like outdoor air
Oxygen may drop and other gases may build up
questions.explanation: A crowded, closed room with poor ventilation is one of the places where oxygen can drop and other gases build up.

questions.question: In open air the usual mix is about
options: 78 nitrogen, 21 oxygen, a little of the rest
21 nitrogen, 78 oxygen, a little of the rest
78 oxygen, 21 carbon dioxide, a little argon
questions.explanation: The steady composition is about 78 cups nitrogen, 21 cups oxygen and a little of the other gases.

questions.question: The caver's device was checking for tools and water.
questions.explanation: False. It was checking the gases in the air around the caver.

questions.question: In closed rooms with poor ventilation, other gases can build up more than usual.
questions.explanation: True. Where air can't move or mix freely, oxygen can drop and other gases can build up.

questions.question: Changes in the air of a closed space are easy to notice right away without any device.
questions.explanation: False. The book says this balance can change 'without anyone noticing right away'.

questions.question: Sealed grain storage bins are mentioned as places where oxygen can drop.
questions.explanation: True. Sealed grain storage bins are one of the examples given.

questions.question: Select the TWO things the caver's device makes sure of.
options: Oxygen is still enough to breathe
Carbon dioxide has not built up too much
questions.explanation: The device checks oxygen is enough and carbon dioxide hasn't built up; nitrogen and argon are not the concern.

questions.question: The book says fire is not a thing but
options: a solid made of hot ash
a gas stored in the fuel
questions.explanation: Fire is a chemical reaction happening continuously between a fuel and oxygen, releasing heat and light.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the three sides of the fire triangle?
questions.explanation: The three requirements for fire are fuel, heat and oxygen.

questions.question: Fire is a reaction between a fuel and which gas in air?
questions.explanation: Fire is a chemical reaction between a fuel and air, specifically oxygen.

questions.question: As fire burns, it releases
questions.explanation: The reaction between fuel and oxygen releases heat and light as it goes.

questions.question: Why do scientists describe the requirements for fire as a triangle?
options: Three people are needed to light it
Removing any one side makes it collapse
questions.explanation: Just as a triangle collapses if you remove one side, fire stops the moment any one condition disappears.

questions.question: A firefighter covers a burning oil pan with a metal lid. Which side of the fire triangle is removed?
questions.explanation: The lid cuts off the air supply, so the fire has no oxygen to react with and goes out.

questions.question: You pour water on a campfire and it goes out. Which side of the fire triangle is removed?
questions.explanation: Water cools the fire below the temperature it needs, so the triangle collapses from the heat side.

questions.question: A gas stove knob is turned OFF and the flame dies. Which side was removed?
questions.explanation: Turning the knob off stops the gas, which is the fuel, so the fire cannot continue.

questions.question: A campfire goes out when all the wood has been used up. Which part of the fire triangle was removed?
questions.explanation: Wood is the fuel. When it is used up, the fire has nothing left to burn.

questions.question: You cover a burning diya with a steel bowl and the flame goes out in a few seconds. Why?
options: The bowl made the diya too cold to burn
The bowl blocked the heat from escaping
The bowl cut off the supply of oxygen
The bowl used up all the fuel inside
questions.explanation: The bowl stops fresh air reaching the flame, so the oxygen runs low and the fire triangle breaks.

questions.question: What happens 'the moment the reaction cannot sustain itself'?
questions.explanation: Fire is a continuous reaction; when it can no longer keep going, the fire simply stops.

questions.question: Sand is thrown over a small fire and it is smothered. Which side of the triangle is most likely removed?
questions.explanation: Like a lid on an oil pan, sand covers the fire and stops air (oxygen) reaching it.

questions.question: Complete the blank: The three things every fire needs are oxygen, ____ and ____.
questions.explanation: Every fire needs oxygen, heat and fuel; these are the three sides of the fire triangle.

questions.question: The book describes fire as an event, not a thing.
questions.explanation: True. Fire is a chemical reaction that keeps happening between fuel and oxygen.

questions.question: Removing any one side of the fire triangle puts the fire out.
questions.explanation: True. Fire collapses the moment any one condition disappears.

questions.question: A fire can keep burning if it has fuel and heat but no oxygen.
questions.explanation: False. All three sides are needed; without oxygen the fire goes out.

questions.question: Pouring water on a campfire mainly removes the fuel.
questions.explanation: False. Water removes the heat side; the wood (fuel) is still there.

questions.question: Select the TWO items that are sides of the fire triangle.
questions.explanation: The triangle has fuel, heat and oxygen. Air pressure and nitrogen are not part of it.

questions.question: A blue flame on a gas stove means the fire is
questions.explanation: A blue flame means plenty of oxygen, efficient burning and more heat.

questions.question: A yellow or orange stove flame means
questions.explanation: A yellow or orange flame means there is not enough oxygen and the fuel isn't burning cleanly.

questions.question: When a flame burns yellow, tiny particles of what are produced?
questions.explanation: With too little oxygen the fuel does not burn cleanly, and tiny particles of soot are produced.

questions.question: Which flame produces MORE heat?
questions.explanation: A blue flame burns efficiently with plenty of oxygen and produces more heat.

questions.question: Your stove flame has turned from blue to yellow. What should you conclude?
options: The stove is producing more heat
There is extra oxygen around it
The fuel is not burning cleanly
The gas is burning very efficiently
questions.explanation: A yellow flame signals too little oxygen: the fuel isn't burning cleanly and soot forms.

questions.question: According to the book, what decides whether a stove flame 'lives or dies'?
questions.explanation: The flame and the air around it work together every second; the air decides whether the flame lives or dies.

questions.question: A blue flame means the fire is getting plenty of oxygen.
questions.explanation: True. Blue means efficient burning with lots of oxygen.

questions.question: An orange flame burns more efficiently than a blue one.
questions.explanation: False. Orange or yellow means not enough oxygen; blue is the efficient flame.

questions.question: Soot is produced when fuel burns cleanly with plenty of oxygen.
questions.explanation: False. Soot forms when there is not enough oxygen and fuel burns unclean.

questions.question: Select the TWO signs that a stove flame is burning efficiently.
questions.explanation: An efficient flame is blue and gives more heat; soot and yellow colour show poor burning.

questions.question: What did miners long ago carry to check whether the air was safe?
questions.explanation: Miners carried oil lamps that gave light and also helped them 'read the air'.

questions.question: A bright, steady lamp flame told miners that
options: the lamp was running out of oil
it was time to turn back
questions.explanation: A bright, steady flame meant the air could support burning and was safe.

questions.question: If a miner's flame became weak or small, it was
options: a signal to light more lamps
a warning that the air had changed
a sign that the air was very fresh
questions.explanation: A weak flame warned miners that something in the air had changed.

questions.question: What would miners do if the lamp flame went out?
options: Light the lamp again and go deeper
Run quickly to finish the work
Wait for the flame to come back
Stop, check and turn back if needed
questions.explanation: A flame going out was a serious signal; miners would stop, check and turn back if needed.

questions.question: Who designed a safer lamp for miners in 1815?
questions.explanation: In 1815, Humphry Davy designed a safer lamp that helped miners detect dangerous conditions underground.

questions.question: In which year was the safer miner's lamp designed?
questions.explanation: The Did You Know box says Humphry Davy designed the safer lamp in 1815.

questions.question: What measures gases in the air for workers today?
questions.explanation: Today, electronic sensors measure gases in the air; long ago a tiny flame did the same job.

questions.question: What does the book mean by 'the lamp didn't just give light, it read the air'?
options: The lamp could print out a gas report
The light made the air easier to see
The lamp warmed the cold mine air
The flame's behaviour showed if the air was safe
questions.explanation: By watching whether the flame was bright, weak or out, miners learned about the air around them.

questions.question: Why is the miners' lamp called 'science in action'?
options: They used observations to stay safe
They did experiments in a laboratory
questions.explanation: Watching the flame and acting on it is using observations to make safe decisions.

questions.question: Which flame sign was the MOST serious for miners?
questions.explanation: A flame that went out was a signal to stop and turn back; a weak flame was only a warning.

questions.question: Long ago, miners had machines that measured gases precisely.
questions.explanation: False. Long before machines could measure gases, miners used oil-lamp flames.

questions.question: Humphry Davy designed a safer miner's lamp in 1815.
questions.explanation: True. This is given in the Did You Know box.

questions.question: If a miner's flame went out, the miners would hurry deeper to finish quickly.
questions.explanation: False. They would stop, check and turn back if needed.

questions.question: Modern electronic sensors do the same job the tiny flame once did.
questions.explanation: True. The Then and Now box compares the oil lamp with the modern oxygen sensor.

questions.question: Select the TWO correct flame signals used by miners.
options: Bright steady flame = air supports burning
Flame goes out = stop and turn back
Weak flame = air is extra rich in oxygen
Bright flame = danger, leave at once
questions.explanation: Bright meant safe, weak meant warning, and a flame going out meant stop and turn back.

questions.question: What does a GENTLE flow of air do to a candle flame?
options: Blows the hot fuel vapour far away
Turns the flame yellow and smoky
Brings fresh oxygen so it burns brighter
Cools it until the flame goes out
questions.explanation: A gentle flow brings fresh oxygen; more oxygen means the fuel burns more efficiently and the flame grows brighter.

questions.question: What does a STRONG blast of air do to a candle flame?
options: Feeds it more oxygen to grow
Adds more wax to the wick
Makes it burn a brighter blue
Cools it and blows the fuel vapour away
questions.explanation: A strong blast cools the flame below the needed temperature and blows the hot fuel vapour away.

questions.question: When you blow out a candle, the fire triangle collapses from which side?
questions.explanation: The strong blast cools the flame below the temperature needed, so the triangle breaks on the heat side.

questions.question: 'Same air, two opposite results.' What does the result depend on?
options: How much nitrogen is in the air
Which side of the triangle is affected
How tall the candle and wick are
What colour the candle wax is
questions.explanation: Gentle air adds oxygen; a strong blast removes heat. The outcome depends on which side of the triangle is affected.

questions.question: Air is what fire needs, so why doesn't blowing hard make the candle brighter?
options: The flame cannot use moving air
The blast removes heat and fuel vapour
The blast removes all the nitrogen
questions.explanation: A strong blast cools the flame and blows the hot fuel vapour away from the burning zone.

questions.question: You gently fan a campfire and it grows bigger. Why?
options: Fanning adds more wood to the fire
Fanning raises the heat of the air
More oxygen makes the fuel burn efficiently
questions.explanation: Like a gentle flow on a candle, fanning brings fresh oxygen so the fuel burns more efficiently.

questions.question: A gentle breeze can make a flame burn brighter and stronger.
questions.explanation: True. A gentle flow of air brings fresh oxygen to the flame.

questions.question: Blowing hard on a candle puts it out by removing all the oxygen.
questions.explanation: False. A strong blast removes heat and fuel vapour; it collapses the triangle from the heat side.

questions.question: A strong blast blows the hot fuel vapour away from the burning zone.
questions.explanation: True. This is one of the two effects of a strong blast.

questions.question: Select the TWO things a strong blast of air does to a flame.
options: Cools the flame below the needed temperature
Blows the hot fuel vapour away
Adds extra fuel to the wick
questions.explanation: A strong blast cools the flame and blows the hot fuel vapour away from the burning zone.

questions.question: What happens when a glass jar is placed over a burning candle?
questions.explanation: The candle uses up the oxygen trapped inside the jar, and once it runs low the flame goes out.

questions.question: What did the glass jar limit to make the flame behave this way?
options: The oxygen available to the flame
The heat of the candle wick
The fuel in the candle wax
questions.explanation: The jar traps a fixed amount of air, so the oxygen runs out and the flame dies.

questions.question: When a candle under a jar goes out, which side of the fire triangle has broken?
questions.explanation: Fuel and heat are still there, but without oxygen the fire triangle breaks.

questions.question: A cold metal spoon held inside the jar gets tiny droplets on it. What are they?
options: Melted wax thrown up by the candle
Oil left behind on the glass jar
Carbon dioxide that turned to liquid
Water from the candle's water vapour
questions.explanation: The droplets are water vapour, one of the gases the candle produces as it burns.

questions.question: As a candle burns, it uses up oxygen and releases
questions.explanation: A candle doesn't just 'burn'; it uses up oxygen and releases carbon dioxide and water vapour instead.

questions.question: Which is TRUE at the moment a candle under a jar goes out?
options: Carbon dioxide inside turned to water
Fuel and heat remain but oxygen has run low
The fuel ran out because the wax melted
The jar cooled the flame below its temperature
questions.explanation: The book says fuel and heat are still there, but without oxygen the triangle breaks.

questions.question: Like the miner's flame, a candle can act as a signal telling us
options: how hot the room has become
how much water vapour is around
whether there is enough oxygen in the air
how much nitrogen is in the air
questions.explanation: The candle uses fire as a signal of whether there is enough oxygen in the air to keep it alive.

questions.question: In the jar investigation, which observation is evidence of a gas the candle produced?
options: The flame getting brighter and taller
The jar becoming lighter to lift
The wax at the top turning black
Droplets of water on the cold spoon
questions.explanation: Water droplets on the spoon show water vapour produced by the burning candle.

questions.question: A candle under a jar goes out because the jar removes the fuel.
questions.explanation: False. The candle uses up the oxygen in the jar; the fuel is still there.

questions.question: Water droplets on the cold spoon come from water vapour the candle produced.
questions.explanation: True. Water vapour is one of the gases released as the candle burns.

questions.question: A burning candle releases oxygen into the jar.
questions.explanation: False. A burning candle uses up oxygen and releases carbon dioxide and water vapour.

questions.question: A candle under a jar uses up the oxygen trapped inside.
questions.explanation: True. Once the oxygen runs low, the flame goes out.

questions.question: Select the TWO things a candle does as it burns.
questions.explanation: A candle uses up oxygen and releases carbon dioxide and water vapour.

questions.question: What causes air pressure?
options: Air molecules bouncing off every surface
Wind blowing from the sea to the land
questions.explanation: Millions of tiny pushes from moving air molecules bouncing off surfaces, every second, is air pressure.

questions.question: In which directions does air push?
options: Up, down, sideways and inward at once
questions.explanation: Air pushes upward, downward, sideways and inward, all at the same time, with equal force.

questions.question: Why don't we usually feel air pressing on our skin?
options: Our skin is too thick to feel it
Air only pushes on hard objects
The pushes from all sides balance out
Air is too light to push anything
questions.explanation: Air pushes on us equally from every direction, so the pushes balance and it feels like no push at all.

questions.question: When the pressure balance breaks, things move toward
questions.explanation: The stronger push wins, so things move toward the side with lower pressure.

questions.question: In the glass-and-card trick, why does the card NOT fall when the glass is turned upside down?
options: Outside air pushes up on the card
The water glues the card to the glass
The glass becomes lighter when inverted
Gravity stops pulling on the water
questions.explanation: Air pushes in all directions, so the outside air pushes upward on the card strongly enough to hold the water in.

questions.question: You blow up a balloon and it becomes firm and round. What pushes outward on its walls?
options: The air outside pushing it into shape
The air pressure inside the balloon
The weight of the rubber stretching
questions.explanation: The air you blew in presses outward on the balloon walls, keeping it firm and round.

questions.question: When you open a sealed packet of chips you hear a hiss. Which way does the air move?
options: Both ways equally, so nothing changes
Outward, because pressure inside is higher
Inward, because packets are low pressure
questions.explanation: Air moves from high to low pressure; the packet's inside is at higher pressure, so air rushes out.

questions.question: If one side of an object has FEWER air molecules than the other, that side
questions.explanation: Fewer molecules means fewer bounces, so that side pushes less and the other side's push wins.

questions.question: The book says the invisible push of air is strong enough to
options: hold up aeroplanes and crush cans
light a candle flame on its own
questions.explanation: Even though we can't feel it, air pressure can hold up aeroplanes and crush cans.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: Air pushes from ____ directions at the same time, which is why we do not feel it.
questions.explanation: Air pushes from all directions at once, and the balanced pushes cancel out.

questions.question: You squeeze a dropper, dip it in water and let go. The water rises in. Which side had lower pressure?
questions.explanation: Squeezing pushed air out, so the inside had fewer molecules and lower pressure; outside air pushed water in.

questions.question: A suction cup sticks to a smooth tile. Which side has lower pressure and what makes it stick?
options: Outside the cup; the tile pulls it in
Inside the cup; the rubber glues itself
Outside the cup; gravity holds it up
Inside the cup; outside air pushes it on
questions.explanation: Pressing the cup pushes air out, so the inside has lower pressure and the outside air presses the cup onto the tile.

questions.question: A bicycle tyre bursts with a loud bang. What happened to the pressure balance?
options: Outside air rushed into the tyre
The tyre air turned into nitrogen
questions.explanation: The air inside was at higher pressure than outside, so when the tyre split it rushed out toward the lower pressure.

questions.question: Air pressure pushes only downward.
questions.explanation: False. Air pushes upward, downward, sideways and inward all at the same time.

questions.question: Billions of air molecules fit in a single breath.
questions.explanation: True. Air molecules are so tiny that billions fit in one breath.

questions.question: We usually notice air's push only when the air is trapped, like in a tyre.
questions.explanation: True. We notice the push when air is trapped, but open air pushes constantly too.

questions.question: Free, open air does not push on anything until it is trapped.
questions.explanation: False. Even free, open air is constantly pushing on everything it touches.

questions.question: Select the TWO true statements about air molecules.
options: They move constantly in random directions
They are too tiny to be seen
They stay still unless wind blows
They can be seen with a magnifying glass
questions.explanation: Air molecules are too tiny to see and are constantly moving and bouncing off surfaces.

questions.question: When you sip through a straw, pulling your cheeks in creates
options: a vacuum in the drink itself
more air molecules in your mouth
questions.explanation: Pulling your cheeks in pulls air out of the straw, leaving fewer molecules and lower pressure in your mouth.

questions.question: What actually moves the drink UP the straw?
options: The straw sucking the liquid by itself
The drink being lighter than air
Outside air pushing on the drink's surface
Your mouth pulling the liquid upward
questions.explanation: Outside air at full pressure pushes harder on the drink than the air in your mouth does, so the drink moves up.

questions.question: Can your mouth pull liquid up a straw by itself?
options: Yes, the tongue lifts the liquid
Yes, the cheeks pull it directly
No, the straw pumps it upward
No, outside air pushes the drink up
questions.explanation: You only lower the pressure in your mouth; the higher outside pressure pushes the drink up.

questions.question: When you breathe in, the space inside your chest expands and
options: air is pulled by the ribs
questions.explanation: Expanding the chest lowers the pressure inside the lungs below the outside pressure.

questions.question: Why does air rush into your lungs when you breathe in?
options: The air outside is always warmer
Outside air is at higher pressure
Your lungs pull it in like a magnet
questions.explanation: Outside air is at higher pressure than the air in your expanded lungs, so it rushes in, like the drink up the straw.

questions.question: Using the same rule, what must happen when you breathe OUT?
options: Pressure stays equal and air flows anyway
Air in the lungs stops moving completely
Lung pressure rises above outside and air flows out
Outside pressure rises and pushes air in
questions.explanation: Air moves from high to low pressure; breathing out makes the lung pressure higher, so air flows out.

questions.question: In which situation might your ears feel blocked and then pop?
questions.explanation: The book lists a fast lift, a mountain road and a plane as places your ears may pop.

questions.question: As you go higher in a plane, what happens to the pressure outside your ears?
options: It drops below the pressure inside
It rises above the pressure inside
questions.explanation: Going higher, the outside air pressure drops, so for a moment the pressure inside the ears is higher.

questions.question: What makes your ears 'pop'?
options: A passage opens and the pressure balances
Air molecules escape from the brain
Your ears make more air inside
questions.explanation: Swallowing or yawning opens a tiny passage in the ear that lets the pressure balance out—pop!

questions.question: Wind from the cool sea to hot land and drink moving up a straw—what do these have in common?
options: Both happen only near the sea
Both need water vapour to work
Air moves from high to low pressure
questions.explanation: In both, air (or liquid pushed by air) moves from the high-pressure side to the low-pressure side.

questions.question: Which action lets the pressure in your ears balance out?
questions.explanation: When you swallow or yawn, a tiny passage inside the ear opens and lets the pressure balance.

questions.question: Your mouth pulls the liquid up the straw all by itself.
questions.explanation: False. Outside air pushing on the drink moves it toward the lower pressure in your mouth.

questions.question: Without a difference in pressure, breathing would not be possible.
questions.explanation: True. Air rushes into the lungs only because the outside pressure is higher.

questions.question: As you go up in a plane, the air pressure outside increases.
questions.explanation: False. As you go higher, the air pressure outside drops.

questions.question: Your ears can detect pressure changes you can't see, hear or feel in any other way.
questions.explanation: True. The book calls ears 'pressure detectors'.

questions.question: Select the TWO situations where the book says your ears may pop.
questions.explanation: A fast lift, a mountain road and a plane are given as examples; the others are not.

questions.question: High above sea level, the air pressure is
questions.explanation: At places high above sea level the air pressure is lower.

questions.question: At high altitude, each breath contains
questions.explanation: Lower pressure means less oxygen is available in each breath, so the body works harder.

questions.question: After weeks of training in the mountains, how does the body adapt?
options: It makes more red blood cells
questions.explanation: The body adapts by making more red blood cells, which carry oxygen around the body.

questions.question: What is the job of red blood cells mentioned in the book?
questions.explanation: Red blood cells help carry oxygen around the body.

questions.question: When athletes return to sea level after mountain training, they
options: use oxygen more effectively and perform better
struggle because there is too little oxygen
lose all the extra red blood cells at once
need oxygen tanks to breathe normally
questions.explanation: Back at higher pressure with more red blood cells, their bodies use oxygen more effectively.

questions.question: What is the percentage of oxygen in air at the summit of Mount Everest?
questions.explanation: Misconception alert: oxygen stays about 21% at any altitude; what drops is the air pressure.

questions.question: What actually causes altitude sickness?
options: Too much nitrogen at the mountain top
The cold turning oxygen into water
Lower air pressure, not lower oxygen percentage
A lower percentage of oxygen in the air
questions.explanation: Lower pressure packs fewer total molecules into each breath; the oxygen percentage does not change.

questions.question: At the summit of Everest, the air pressure is about
questions.explanation: Air pressure at the summit is about 1/3 of that at sea level.

questions.question: Why do climbers gasp and need oxygen tanks on Everest?
options: Fewer total air molecules in each breath
Oxygen is missing from mountain air
Nitrogen replaces oxygen when it is cold
Their red blood cells stop working
questions.explanation: Lower pressure means fewer molecules per breath, so less oxygen reaches the body even though the percentage is the same.

questions.question: How long do athletes spend training in the mountains before the body adapts, according to the book?
questions.explanation: After spending several weeks training in the mountains, the body makes more red blood cells.

questions.question: Mount Everest's air has a much lower percentage of oxygen than sea-level air.
questions.explanation: False. Oxygen stays at about 21% at any altitude; the air pressure is what drops.

questions.question: At the summit of Everest, air pressure is about one third of that at sea level.
questions.explanation: True. The book gives the figure of about 1/3.

questions.question: Athletes train in the mountains because the air there has more oxygen in each breath.
questions.explanation: False. Mountain air gives LESS oxygen per breath, which makes the body adapt.

questions.question: After weeks at high altitude, the body makes more red blood cells.
questions.explanation: True. This is how the body adapts to less oxygen per breath.

questions.question: Select the TWO true statements about air at high altitude.
options: Fewer air molecules fit in each breath
Oxygen drops to about 10% of the air
The air is mostly carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Pressure is lower so each breath holds fewer molecules; the oxygen percentage stays about 21%.

questions.question: What is wind?
options: Oxygen moving out of the lungs
Air flowing from high to low pressure
Air standing still over hot land
questions.explanation: Air always flows from high pressure toward low pressure; that flowing air is wind.

questions.question: When a surface heats up, the air above it
questions.explanation: Warm air spreads out and rises, leaving fewer molecules near the ground.

questions.question: When warm air rises, what happens to the pressure near the ground?
questions.explanation: Rising warm air leaves a gap with fewer molecules and less weight pressing down, so pressure drops.

questions.question: In a cooler area, the air stays
options: spread out, so pressure is high
dense and heavy, so pressure is high
light and thin, so pressure is low
warm and rising, so pressure is low
questions.explanation: Cool air is dense and heavy, so the pressure stays high there.

questions.question: Circle the right word: The air over the hot land will
questions.explanation: Hot land warms the air above it, which spreads out and rises.

questions.question: Circle the right word: Rising air over the hot land creates ____ pressure over the land.
questions.explanation: Rising air leaves fewer molecules near the ground, so low pressure forms over the land.

questions.question: Circle the right word: The air over the cool sea will
questions.explanation: Cool air over the sea stays dense and heavy.

questions.question: Circle the right word: Dense air over the cool sea creates ____ pressure over the sea.
questions.explanation: Dense, heavy air means high pressure sits over the sea.

questions.question: Circle the right word: Wind blows from
questions.explanation: Air always moves from high pressure toward low pressure.

questions.question: What drives air across huge distances to make wind?
questions.explanation: Wind is air moving across huge distances, driven by heat.

questions.question: A bottle left in bright sunlight feels like it wants to pop its cap, while one in the shade doesn't. Why?
options: Warm air inside spreads out and pushes harder
Sunlight adds more air into the bottle
The shade bottle has lost all its air
questions.explanation: Heat makes the air inside warm and spread out, so it presses harder on the cap than the cool air in the shaded bottle.

questions.question: On a cloudy day, the wind near the coast is weaker than on a sunny day. Why?
options: Clouds add many more air molecules over the land
Land heats less, so the pressure difference is smaller
Clouds physically block the wind from blowing
The sea becomes much hotter than the land does
questions.explanation: With less sunshine the land does not heat as much, air rises less, and the high-low pressure difference is smaller.

questions.question: Which is the DIRECT cause of wind?
options: Trees waving their branches back and forth
Clouds pushing the air down to the ground
A difference in air pressure between two places
The spinning of the Earth under the air
questions.explanation: Air flows from high to low pressure; that pressure difference, created by uneven heating, is what makes wind.

questions.question: You open a fridge door. Using the book's rule, which way does air move?
options: Warm room air rushes in because it is denser
No air moves because the fridge is sealed
Air moves both ways in exactly equal amounts
Cool, dense fridge air spills out toward the warm room
questions.explanation: Cool air is dense and heavy (higher pressure), so it flows toward the warmer, lower-pressure air of the kitchen.

questions.question: Wind blows from low pressure toward high pressure.
questions.explanation: False. Air always flows from high pressure toward low pressure.

questions.question: Warm air rises and leaves lower pressure behind it.
questions.explanation: True. Rising warm air leaves a gap with fewer molecules, so pressure drops.

questions.question: Cool air is dense and heavy, so pressure stays high where air is cool.
questions.explanation: True. In cooler areas, air stays dense and heavy and the pressure is high.

questions.question: The air over a hot surface sinks toward the ground.
questions.explanation: False. Air over a hot surface warms, spreads out and rises.

questions.question: Select the TWO things that happen over hot land.
questions.explanation: Hot land warms the air, which rises and leaves low pressure; dense air and high pressure belong to the cool sea.

questions.question: By midday, what happens over the hot land at the coast?
options: Air rises and low pressure forms
Air sinks and high pressure forms
questions.explanation: The land absorbs hours of sunshine, air over it rises, and low pressure forms over the land.

questions.question: Compared with land, the sea heats up
questions.explanation: Water takes much longer to warm than sand or soil, so the sea stays cooler.

questions.question: In the afternoon, a sea breeze blows from
questions.explanation: High pressure over the sea plus low pressure over the land makes cool sea air rush toward the land.

questions.question: Which city is NOT listed in the book as one that experiences the sea breeze?
questions.explanation: The book names Mumbai, Chennai, Kochi and Puri, all coastal cities.

questions.question: Complete the sea breeze 'formula': High pressure over the sea + ____ = sea breeze.
questions.explanation: High pressure over the sea and low pressure over the land makes cool sea air rush toward the land.

questions.question: The book calls the monsoon
options: a sea breeze without any water
a giant version of a sea breeze
a tiny version of a sea breeze
questions.explanation: The monsoon is like a sea breeze but thousands of kilometres wide and carrying enormous water vapour.

questions.question: Every summer, where does a massive low-pressure area form?
questions.explanation: The Indian landmass heats intensely, air rises, and a massive low-pressure area forms over India.

questions.question: In the monsoon, moist ocean air flows
questions.explanation: Moist ocean air flows northward toward the land, like a sea breeze thousands of kilometres wide.

questions.question: Where does the moist air rise, cool and drop its rain, according to the book?
questions.explanation: As moist air rises over the Western Ghats it cools, water vapour condenses into clouds and rain falls.

questions.question: What drives the monsoon, according to the book?
options: The sea becoming hotter than the land
Land and ocean heating at different speeds
questions.explanation: The monsoon is driven by the difference in how fast land and the ocean heat up.

questions.question: How is the monsoon DIFFERENT from an afternoon sea breeze?
options: It is driven by the cold of winter instead of summer heat
It happens only in the evening after the land cools down
It is thousands of km wide and carries far more water vapour
It blows from the hot land out toward the cooler sea
questions.explanation: Both work the same way, but the monsoon is thousands of kilometres wide and carries enormous amounts of water vapour.

questions.question: What condenses into clouds when the moist monsoon air rises and cools?
questions.explanation: As the moist air cools, water vapour condenses into clouds and rain falls.

questions.question: The book says the cool afternoon sea breeze is made entirely by
questions.explanation: Every coastal city's afternoon breeze is 'made entirely by air pressure'.

questions.question: Water takes much longer to warm than sand or soil.
questions.explanation: True. This is why the sea stays cooler than the land by midday.

questions.question: In the afternoon the sea breeze blows from the land toward the sea.
questions.explanation: False. Cool sea air rushes toward the hot land, so the breeze blows from sea to land.

questions.question: In summer the Indian Ocean heats up faster than the Indian landmass.
questions.explanation: False. The ocean heats more slowly, so it stays relatively cooler with high pressure over it.

questions.question: Moist monsoon air cools as it rises over the Western Ghats.
questions.explanation: True. Rising air cools, water vapour condenses, and rain falls.

questions.question: Select the TWO cities the book names as experiencing the sea breeze.
questions.explanation: Mumbai, Chennai, Kochi and Puri are the coastal cities named.

questions.question: Select the TWO true statements about the monsoon.
options: High pressure sits over the Indian Ocean
Ocean air flows southward away from India
Dry air sinks over the Western Ghats
questions.explanation: Hot land gives low pressure; the cooler ocean has high pressure; moist air flows north and rises over the Ghats.

questions.question: Which gas makes up the largest part of the air we breathe?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is about 78% of air, the largest part.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: The gas in air that does almost nothing and is present in the smallest usable trace is ____.
questions.explanation: Argon is a small trace that doesn't react with anything.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: When air over a surface gets warm, it ____ and leaves a gap of lower pressure behind.
questions.explanation: Warm air rises, leaving fewer molecules near the ground and lower pressure.

questions.question: Fill in the blank: When hot air over land rises and moves away, it creates a ____ pressure zone that cooler air rushes in to fill.
questions.explanation: Rising hot air leaves low pressure, and nearby cooler high-pressure air rushes in.

questions.question: Nitrogen makes up 78% of air but your body does not use it. Why is it still important?
options: It makes the air easier to see
It dilutes oxygen to a safe level
It gives the body extra energy
It helps plants make their food
questions.explanation: Nitrogen keeps oxygen from being too concentrated; pure oxygen would be toxic and things would catch fire too easily.

questions.question: On the live tracker app mentioned in the book, what can you watch during the monsoon season?
questions.explanation: The tracker shows wind and clouds moving; in monsoon season you can watch the monsoon clouds travel across India.

questions.question: Which belief from the chapter is a MISCONCEPTION?
options: A blue flame gets plenty of oxygen
Air moves from high to low pressure
Nitrogen is the largest part of air
Everest air has a lower oxygen percentage
questions.explanation: Oxygen stays about 21% at any altitude; it is the pressure that drops. The other three statements are true.

questions.question: Which pair correctly matches an example with the air property it shows?
options: Candle under a jar — air supports burning
Straw — air is a mixture of gases
questions.explanation: The candle shows air supports burning; sea breeze and straw show pressure; argon welding shows air is a mixture.

questions.question: Which word from the word box completes: 'Air pushes from ____ directions at the same time'?
questions.explanation: Air pushes from all directions at once, which is why we don't feel it on our skin.

questions.question: Which THEN and NOW pair does the book give for reading the air?
options: Oil lamp then, oxygen sensor now
questions.explanation: The Then and Now box compares the miners' oil lamp with the modern electronic oxygen sensor.

questions.question: The closing paragraph says air helps us breathe, feeds flames and pushes on everything.
questions.explanation: True. It also says air turns into the winds and rains that shape our lives.

questions.question: The book says air is only 'in action' when there is a storm.
questions.explanation: False. From a candle flame to a beach breeze, air is always in action, everywhere.

questions.question: The word box is: argon, heat, rises, low, all, fuel, water vapour, carbon dioxide. Which TWO words are NOT needed for any blank?
questions.explanation: The blanks use all, rises, argon, heat, fuel and low; water vapour and carbon dioxide are extra.

questions.question: Select the TWO events explained by a difference in air pressure.
options: A drink rising up a straw
questions.explanation: Straws and sea breezes work by pressure differences; flame colour and welding are about burning and gas use.

questions.question: According to the closing paragraph, select TWO ways air is 'in action'.
questions.explanation: Air helps us breathe, feeds flames, pushes on everything, and becomes winds and rains.
